content: A vaginal septum is a congenital partition within the vaginal canal. This partition can be classified as either longitudinal or transverse, depending on its orientation. Longitudinal Vaginal Septum Double Vagina A longitudinal vaginal septum arises during embryogenesis due to incomplete fusion of the lower segments of the two Müllerian ducts. This results in the formation of a double vagina. In some cases, there may also be associated duplications of other structures derived from the Müllerian ducts, such as a double cervix, a uterine septum, or a condition known as uterus didelphys (double uterus). Individuals with a longitudinal vaginal septum may remain asymptomatic and unaware of the condition. However, if dyspareunia (pain during sexual intercourse) occurs, the septum can be surgically resected to alleviate symptoms. Transverse Vaginal Septum A transverse vaginal septum forms during embryogenesis when the fusion between the Müllerian ducts and the urogenital sinus is incomplete or improper. A complete transverse septum obstructs menstrual flow, leading to primary amenorrhea (absence of menstruation). The accumulation of menstrual blood and debris behind the septum is referred to as cryptomenorrhea. In cases where the transverse septum is incomplete, it may cause dyspareunia or complications during labor. Surgical incision of the septum is the definitive treatment to resolve these issues. It is essential to differentiate a transverse vaginal septum from other conditions that delay the development of secondary sexual characteristics. These conditions include constitutional delay of puberty, hypopituitarism, delayed puberty, and chromosomal abnormalities such as Turner syndrome and Noonan syndrome.
